data.title: Four financial firms approve merger
data.description:
SHARE SWAP: First Securities Investment Trust Co would be the surviving entity due to its larger asset base and stronger operating performance, executives said

Four state-owned financial holding companies yesterday approved a plan to merge their investment trust subsidiaries into a larger, more competitive asset manager, aiming to cut operating costs, broaden product offerings and improve Taiwan’s position as a regional asset management hub.

The planned merger aims to achieve economies of scale by pooling resources, technology and distribution networks, allowing the combined company to improve operating efficiency and compete more effectively, executives said.

First Financial Holding Co (第一金控), Mega Financial Holding Co (兆豐金控), Taiwan Cooperative Financial Holding Co (合庫金控) and Hua Nan Financial Holdings Co (華南金控) said their boards and those of their investment trust subsidiaries had approved the deal.

First Securities Investment Trust Co (第一金投信) would be the surviving entity because of its larger asset base and stronger operating performance, they said.

The merger, which requires regulatory approval, is planned for Jan. 1, 2028.

First Securities Investment Trust would absorb Mega International Investment Trust Co (兆豐國際投信), Taiwan Cooperative Securities Investment Trust Co (合作金庫投信) and Hua Nan Investment Trust Co (華南永昌投信), with all of the approximately 370 employees to have the option to stay on.

The parent companies would hold stakes of 50.3 percent, 30.4 percent, 9.8 percent and 9.5 percent respectively in the combined firm.

The transaction would be conducted through a share swap, with First Securities Investment Trust issuing about 59.3 million new common shares.

The new company would retain the First Securities Investment Trust name, with First Financial controlling appointments to its top management positions, First Financial Holding president Frank Fang (方螢基) said.

The combined company is expected to benefit from lower operating costs and more effective use of the four groups’ distribution networks, Fang said, adding that a broader range of investment products should help improve profitability and shareholder returns.

First Securities Investment Trust president Richard Kao (高子敬) said that the entity’s assets under management would total about NT$500 billion (US$15.38 billion), including publicly offered funds and discretionary investment mandates.

The company aims to increase assets in publicly offered funds by 15 percent annually and those in discretionary investment mandates by 10 percent, Kao said.

To achieve those targets, it plans to develop products focused on retirement planning, sustainable investment, overseas asset allocation and wealthy clients, he said, adding that it intends to pursue opportunities arising from the government’s push to establish Taiwan as an Asian asset management hub.

The combined publicly offered fund assets of the four merging firms would rank about 12th among Taiwan’s investment trust firms and the merged entity would aim to break into the top 10, he said.

The merged company would have seven directors and two supervisors.

First Financial would appoint four directors and one supervisor, while each of the other three financial holding companies would appoint one director.

Mega Financial would appoint one supervisor.

The four merging companies pledged to protect employee and customer rights during the integration.

First Securities Investment Trust would assume responsibility for existing customers, whose rights would remain protected under applicable regulations.

data.title: TSMC seeks factory-equipment alternatives
data.description:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) is exploring alternatives to rare earth components in factory equipment, three people familiar with the matter said, aiming to reduce the risk that Beijing’s export controls could disrupt operations at plants that make the world’s most advanced chips.

The move underscores how China’s grip on rare earths has become a vulnerability for the global semiconductor industry after the country last year put some rare earth materials, magnets and related processing technology under export controls, requiring licences.

Rare earth magnets are commonly used in motors that power moving parts in industrial equipment, including machinery in highly automated factories such as those operated by TSMC.

A shortage of such specialized parts could disrupt chip production for customers in smartphone, artificial intelligence system, data center and defense supply chains.

TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, has surveyed suppliers on using rare earth-free motors in factory-automation equipment, three industry executives briefed by the company on its plans said.

One of the people said the effort was driven by concerns about potential supply disruptions from China.

The discussions remain in the early stages and have not yet resulted in a broad rollout of rare earth-free equipment, two of the people said.

The Taiwanese company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

TSMC’s efforts follow statements from Taiwan and the US that they would begin looking for ways to reduce their reliance on Chinese rare earth and critical-mineral supply chains.

In June, American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene said that the US is working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and build more resilient supply chains.

Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) in February said that the government would support the Industrial Technology Research Institute (工研院) to develop rare earth technologies, with plans to establish a pilot production line within three years that could meet an estimated 50 percent of the nation’s domestic demand.

data.title: Micron announces a new profit-sharing program
data.description:
STOCK, CASH: Quarterly profit-sharing bonuses would supplement payments under the Incentive Pay Plan, offering ‘transparency’ and ‘predictability,’ an executive said

Micron Memory Taiwan Co (台灣美光) yesterday unveiled a new profit-sharing program and structural wage hikes as part of its efforts to build a predictable and transparent compensation framework in response to feedback from unions.

The memorychip maker, a subsidiary of US-based Micron Technology Inc, announced the major compensation structural overhaul during an online news conference following a milestone agreement with the union representing more than 10,000 workers at its Taichung facility.

Under the new framework, quarterly profit-sharing bonuses would supplement payments under the Incentive Pay Plan (IPP), the company said.

The IPP formula has also been substantially enhanced, it said.

“Profit-sharing mechanisms are common among Asian companies, but they are rarely seen among American technology firms,” Micron Memory Taiwan chairman Donghui Lu (盧東暉) told the news conference. “This approach offers transparency and, to a certain degree, predictability.”

The new mechanism is to take effect in fiscal 2027 and apply to eligible employees in Micron Technology’s global workforce.

Quarterly net income minus forecast capital expenditure for the following quarter would be the basis for calculating profit-sharing bonuses, the company said.

The payout will be distributed equally between stock — subject to one-year vesting — and cash, it said.

Following its annual wage adjustments, Micron Memory Taiwan is to implement another structural payroll increase in an extensive way to avoid salary inversion.

Previously, Micron Memory Taiwan’s wage hikes primarily targeted entry-level personnel and newcomers.

The company hopes to implement the adjustments by Lunar New Year next year, it said.

Micron Memory Taiwan also plans to increase shift differential pay from December. The monthly allowance for day shifts would triple to NT$4,500 (US$138.43), while the allowance for evening shifts would increase to 15 percent of their regular pay, and night shift workers would receive a 20 percent shift differential, it said.

After the adjustments, the conditional top-end compensation for an entry-level engineer would be nearly NT$4 million in fiscal 2027, up from NT$1.45 million in fiscal 2025, while the amount for mid-to-senior-tier engineers is projected at NT$6 million, up from more than NT$2 million, the Taichung union said.

The projections include stock awards and employer retirement contributions.

Micron Memory Taiwan said it would increase its employer pension contribution rate to 10 percent of workers’ regular pay from 8 percent to retain talent.

Representatives of the company’s Taoyuan union yesterday held a one-day strike over accusations that company management had failed to disclose its profit-sharing ratio.

The Taoyuan union is demanding that the allocation be set at 15 percent of Micron Technology’s global operating profit.

data.title: Musk might affect SpaceX-Tesla talks
data.description:
Elon Musk’s public endorsement this week of a potential US$3.5 trillion merger between SpaceX and Tesla has rattled some insiders involved in the discussions, who worry his comments could invite shareholder scrutiny and delay the process by several weeks, a person with direct knowledge of the talks said.

The disclosure created a “mess” for the process, as it could lead to questions about how well Tesla shareholders’ interests would be represented, the person said.

The concerns reflect similarities some participants see with Tesla’s 2016 acquisition of SolarCity, which sparked years of litigation over Musk’s role in the deal.

Musk, who serves as chief executive officer of SpaceX and Tesla, and owns significant stakes in each company, this week told investors that the two companies were examining what would be the largest corporate transaction in history and revealed that both had formed special committees to evaluate it.

The parties have hired advisers, but discussions are at an early stage, three sources familiar with the matter said.

SpaceX approached Tesla in recent weeks and the companies have been discussing a range of transaction structures, including a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla or a merger under a newly formed holding company, the person familiar with the matter said.

They are weighing different forms of merger consideration, including an all-stock deal, the person said.

In related-party transactions such as a SpaceX-Tesla merger, independent board members typically oversee the process to safeguard public shareholders’ interests.

That issue loomed large in Tesla’s 2016 acquisition of SolarCity, which triggered years of litigation after shareholders alleged the world’s richest man had influenced the process to bail out his investment in the struggling rooftop solar company.

At the time, Musk owned about 22 percent of both Tesla and SolarCity, which was founded by his cousins.

Shareholders argued that Musk’s involvement and public support undermined the deal’s fairness.

Central to the case were claims that despite his minority stake, Musk was a controlling shareholder of Tesla due to his ties to board members and domineering style.

The Delaware Supreme Court later said that plaintiffs’ contention of the absence of an independent committee, together with “certain other facts concerning Musk’s involvement in and public support for the transaction,” warranted the finding of unfair dealing.

The courts ultimately upheld the acquisition as fair, although it took several years for the case to be resolved and Tesla directors settled allegations for US$60 million.

Musk owns nearly one-fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.

On Tuesday’s call with investors, Musk said that as a conflicted party, he cannot be part of the discussions of the special committees.

Advisers are also in contact with his lawyers to ensure Musk is recused from the merger discussions, the source familiar with the talks said.

data.title: Egis and SiPearl ink deal
data.description:
Egis Technology Inc (神盾) yesterday signed a strategic partnership with French processor designer SiPearl to jointly develop central processing units (CPU), targeting high-performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI) and data center applications.

The partnership links Egis’ ARM-based Mobius100 (M100) CPU project with SiPearl, combining Taiwanese and French technology and commercial resources to advance processor development, Egis said in a statement.

Egis, which started as a fingerprint sensor designer, has expanded its product portfolio through its subsidiaries into silicon intellectual property, universal chiplet interconnect express technology, advanced packaging and server CPUs.

As AI applications diversify and expand into more vertical industries, Egis has stepped up its efforts to develop chiplet technology and heterogeneous integration, with investments made about two years ago now beginning to bear fruit, the company said.

Egis’ 3-nanometer chiplet is expected to tape out in the first quarter of next year, with mass production slated for the second half of 2028, Egis chairman Steve Ro (羅森洲) told reporters on the sidelines of a signing ceremony for the SiPearl collaboration.

Egis’ chiplets were mainly developed through its subsidiary Alcor Micro (安國).

The partnership with SiPearl would help it expand into European and Middle Eastern markets, with cooperation on second and third-generation products already being planned, Ro said.

The broader roadmap extends across nearly four generations through 2035, while the group is also planning a 12-nanometer AI chip, he said.

SiPearl is a French start-up developing high-performance CPUs for supercomputing, AI and data centers.

The company previously raised 130 million euros (US$146 million), with investors including Cathay Venture Inc (國泰創投), a venture capital arm of Cathay Financial Holding Co (國泰金控).

“The partnership with Egis and Alcor Micro would deepen technology cooperation between Taiwan and Europe, and help develop advanced, resilient hardware solutions for global HPC, AI and data center markets,” SiPearl chief executive officer Philippe Notton said.

Egis plans to center its CPU development work on the latest ARM architecture and build a broader partner ecosystem with Taiwanese suppliers from foundry, chip packaging and CPU customers, Ro said.

The company aims to advance technology development and business opportunities through closer cooperation among industry players, he added.

Through its chiplet and design service businesses, the group has received strong market interest in specialized AI applications and plans to target opportunities in agentic AI, servers and vertical industries, Alcor Micro senior special assistant Cindy Chen (陳巧昕) said.

Beyond Europe, the Middle East and the US, the group also maintains close cooperation with customers and partners in Japan and South Korea, Chen said.

data.title: Bedmaker
data.description: A worker makes a traditional woven bed, known as a “charpai,” at a workshop in Peshawar, Pakistan, yesterday. The handmade beds are sold in various designs and qualities in local markets for 4,500 to 15,000 Pakistani rupees (US$16.21 to US$54.04).

data.title: Powerchip expects more price hikes
data.description:
SUPPLY CRUNCH: Powerchip said it expects price hikes this quarter to be 30 percent, following a rise of 23 percent last quarter, to address persistent capacity constraints

Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp (力積電) is negotiating with customers to further hike prices by 10 to 20 percent next year, the logic and memory chipmaker said yesterday, citing persistent capacity constraints across the industry.

The company said it would prioritize capacity allocation for customers under long-term supply agreements with fixed volumes and pricing.

Last quarter, Powerchip raised prices by 23 percent from the previous quarter, and expects another 30 percent increase this quarter, it said.

“Provided that artificial intelligence [AI] momentum remains strong, we hold a highly optimistic outlook for 2027 revenue and profitability,” Powerchip president Martin Chu (朱憲國) said at an earnings conference.

The company also unveiled a new capacity expansion plan for the next three to five years, saying that it is scouting a site to build a small-scale chip facility in Taiwan, Japan or Singapore.

The new plant would focus on expanding advanced packaging-related technologies, including post-wafer-finish (PWF) service, interposers used in advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging and integrated passive devices (IPD), which are used in AI-related applications, it said.

“We have to expand clean room space to address strong customer demand for those technologies,” Powerchip chairman Brian Shieh (謝再居) said.

Demand for IPD would surge to as many as 50,000 wafers a month in the second half of next year, exceeding its current capacity of 10,000 wafers per month, he said.

To mitigate capital expenditure risks, the company aims to secure 30 to 60 percent of funding for new production line expansions from customers via leasing or prepayments, Shieh said.

Micron Technology Inc has set a precedent by fully funding the manufacturing equipment for Taiwan’s PWF mid-to-back-end packaging expansion through prepayments, he said.

Powerchip is poised to become the world’s sole memory manufacturer producing legacy DRAM from DDR1 to DDR3, utilizing 63-nanometer to 20-nanometer process technologies, Shieh said.

Those technologies are projected to have an extended lifecycle of 10 to 15 years, he said.

The company attributed the ongoing supply crunch to aggressive AI server buildouts, which have spurred massive demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and squeezed mature DDR3 and DDR4 DRAM production.

“As major memory makers aggressively reallocate capacity to HBM and exit mature DRAM, we expect supply tightness for customers,” Chu said. “We anticipate that our niche DRAM foundry pricing will remain robust, showing no signs of a downward adjustment.”

Powerchip attributed the mild pricing weakness in DDR3 DRAM to a temporary supply influx, driven by an enterprise refresh cycle where outdated computers were replaced with AI-capable models.

This pricing softness is expected to be short-lived, the company said.

The company expects revenue to expand by a double-digit percentage sequentially this quarter, after revenue expanded 23 percent last quarter.

Net profit last quarter almost doubled to NT$6.5 billion (US$200 million), from NT$3.29 billion in the previous quarter. That reversed a loss of NT$2.73 billion in the third quarter last year.

Earnings per share rose to NT$1.38 last quarter from NT$0.76 in the previous quarter, while gross margin improved to 48 percent from 28 percent a quarter earlier.

data.title: Moody’s upgrades TSMC credit rating
data.description:
Moody’s Ratings yesterday upgraded Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC, 台積電) credit rating to “Aa2” from “Aa3,” citing its technological leadership in advanced chipmaking, exceptionally strong financial position and strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

The agency also revised its outlook for TSMC from “positive” to “stable,” reflecting expectations that the world’s largest contract chipmaker would maintain its dominant foundry position and robust financial profile over the next two to three years.

The upgrade applies to senior unsecured debt issued by TSMC’s wholly owned subsidiaries, TSMC Arizona Corp and TSMC Global Ltd, and guaranteed by TSMC, Moody’s said.

With the company’s technological edge, manufacturing excellence, diversified customer base and sustained AI demand, TSMC’s revenue is forecast to grow 30 to 45 percent annually over the next 12 to 18 months, the agency said.

TSMC reported 51 percent year-on-year revenue growth in the third quarter, with advanced technologies of 7 nanometers and below accounting for 79 percent of revenue, company data showed.

The company’s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) margin are projected to rise to about 75 percent over the next 12 to 18 months, up from 72 percent last year, Moody’s said, citing higher capacity utilization and productivity gains that offset costs associated with new technologies and overseas facilities.

Despite rising investment needs, TSMC is expected to maintain positive free cash flow and a strong net cash position, it said.

The company’s adjusted debt-to-EBITDA ratio is projected to remain at about 0.3 times, reflecting low leverage, it said.

As of Sept. 30, TSMC held about NT$4 trillion (US$123.1 billion) in cash and marketable securities, enough to cover short-term debt, projected capital spending and dividends over the next 12 months, Moody’s said.

However, as semiconductor manufacturing is capital-intensive and cyclical, it requires continued heavy investment in technology and production capacity in the US, Japan and Germany, the agency said.

A further upgrade in TSMC’s credit rating is unlikely in the near term given the company’s substantial investment needs and the geographic concentration of its manufacturing operations. Its rating is also closely linked to Taiwan’s sovereign rating, because most of its production facilities remain in Taiwan, Moody’s said.

However, a downgrade could follow if the company faces a material loss of technological leadership or market share, sustained deterioration in profitability and cash flow, or investment and shareholder payouts that significantly weaken its net cash position, the agency said.

data.title: Semiconductor industry’s electricity use hits record
data.description:
Electricity consumption by Taiwan’s semiconductor industry topped 4.5 terawatt-hours (TWh) for the first time last month, a record driven by stronger-than-expected demand for artificial intelligence (AI), the Taiwan Research Institute (TRI, 台綜院) said yesterday.

As AI technologies develop rapidly and the demand for computing power grows, global demand for cutting-edge chips, advanced packaging and high-performance chips continues to rise, pushing up the industry’s electricity consumption, the institute said in a statement.

Nationwide, electricity consumption by high-voltage and extra-high-voltage industrial users rose 1.76 percent year-on-year last month, while consumption by manufacturers rose 1.96 percent and that by the semiconductor industry rose 11.55 percent — returning to double-digit growth, it said.

The economic monitoring indicator for the power industry remained at “red,” marking robust activity for the 18th consecutive month, the institute said.

Strong production in the high-tech sector has gradually spurred investment demand in other industries, boosting exports, production and corporate investment, and supporting rapid economic growth, which the institute estimates grew 12.6 percent last month.

The TRI forecast that the semiconductor industry’s annual electricity consumption would exceed 50TWh this year, as AI-related business opportunities expand from high-end chips to servers, equipment, materials and key components, benefiting investment and production across the supply chain.

The chemical materials and textile industries continued to show “blue” monitoring readings, signaling contraction, although for different reasons.

The chemical materials industry remained under pressure from global petrochemical overcapacity and a slow recovery in demand, while the textile industry faced weak international end-market demand and price competition, which continued to weigh on orders and production, the institute said.

data.title: TSMC slows construction after accident kills four
data.description:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) is suspending some construction work after an accident at one of its building sites in southern Taiwan led to the deaths of four workers.

The incident took place on Tuesday during steel structure construction at TSMC’s Fab 22 in Kaohsiung, the company said.

Workers fell from a height while performing steel structure hoisting and installation, a report from the Central News Agency said.

A cause might be aged bolts, it said, citing a preliminary assessment by the Southern Taiwan Science Park Bureau.

The bureau said that work would only resume after Shang Hao Machinery Co (上昊機械), the four deceased workers’ employer, submits an improvement plan that passes review.

The bureau added that penalties would be determined based on the investigation and relevant occupational safety laws.

The construction site underwent three labor inspections last year and 18 this year, including a steel structure inspection on July 8, resulting in two other contractors total receiving fines of NT$210,000 (US$6,467), the bureau said.

TSMC said it immediately suspended work at Kaohsiung and halted similar steel structure construction at all of its sites across Taiwan while the company works with authorities to determine the cause of the accident.

The incident, which Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) reported as the deadliest accident since construction began at the Kaohsiung site, comes as TSMC ratchets up production capacity to keep up with surging demand for advanced chips needed for artificial intelligence.

The Kaohsiung complex is one of TSMC’s key leading-edge manufacturing hubs — along with the company’s facilities in Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科學園區) — with 2-nanometer process technology needed to manufacture high-performance chips to maximize computing power for data centers.

Additional reporting by CNA
